name: Naphthalene Violet
lede: Naphthalene Violet is a grayed reddish-purple named for naphthalene, the coal-tar hydrocarbon that also gave its name to mothballs and to naphthalene yellow and green.

sections.title: Another coal-tar name
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 color book places this value on plate XXXVII, hue 61″, tone k, and the ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 files it as block 242, dark reddish purple [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[dark-hyssop-violet]] and [[dusky-auricula-purple]], at 4.7 and 5 ΔE, with [[slate-purple]] a close third at 5.1, a touch lighter and purpler [1]. What the original dye or pigment looked like, and who first applied the name, is undocumented in the sources consulted here [1].

Compare [[mauve|Mauve]] and [[plum|Plum]] for other grayed purples from the same dye-chemistry era [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive of 23,781 paintings finds a color within six units of this one in 43, about 0.2 percent, as photographed [2]. The earliest is Gentile da Fabriano's King David Plays the Harp (1423), and the color is nearly three times more common in paintings from the 1900s than across the archive as a whole [2]. Gustave Caillebotte carries it in three of his dated works, a strong lift for one painter [2]. The match is a screen-color comparison across aged, varnished paintings, not a pigment identification [2].
